top.titre: Hard to Fool: A Bounded LLM Research Loop for Quantitative Finance, and What Two Dozen Campaigns Found
top.extrait: Agentic research loops that let a language model propose a change, run a fixed experiment and keep whatever improves the metric work well in machine learning. In trading research the same loop is a machine for producing false discoveries: a backtest that "improves the metric" is, by default, overfit, look-ahead, a multiple-comparisons artifact, cost-free, or market drift wearing a strategy.

top.titre: Multidimensional Views Behind Target-Price Revisions: An LLM-Based Representation of Analyst Outlooks
top.extrait: A target price compresses an analyst's multidimensional views into a single number. We propose an LLM-based text representation that extracts these views from research reports as question-based outlook scores with supporting evidence.

top.titre: Neural Realized Measures: Forecast-Supervised Intraday Aggregation for Volatility Forecasting
top.extrait: High-frequency volatility forecasting typically separates measurement from prediction: intraday observations are first compressed into a daily realized measure using a fixed aggregation rule, and the resulting statistic is then passed to a forecasting model. This conventional pipeline therefore treats measure construction as forecast-agnostic preprocessing.

top.extrait: Researchers ask large language model (LLM) research agents whether a forecasting model beats a static benchmark, a verdict that real data cannot check. We treat the agent as a statistical test and score pre-specified runs of three frontier models and one open-weight model in simulated worlds with a planted signal.

top.titre: Thinking Fast, Trading Late: System One Decision Models vs the Market
top.extrait: Large language models (LLMs) read company news at scale, and backtests suggest that their readings predict stock returns. We ask how much of that predictability survives a test that rules out look-ahead, memorization and selection.

top.extrait: Financial research agents can generate and monitor trading rules faster than a human can document the resulting selection process. Candidates appear at data-dependent times, weak rules are abandoned, and promising ones are watched until they cross a reporting threshold.
